coachMessages.text: Green has played the centre column three times. Gray is about to move — the simplest good reply is often just to play directly above Green's last disc.

slides.infoProse: Allen calls this 'I play where you play': surprisingly often, the best move for a player is to play directly above the opponent's just-played disc. It sounds too simple to matter, but when you can recognise that imitation is good enough, it makes finding a strong move very easy — no deep calculation required.

coachMessages.text: After both sides raced up the centre column, Green shifted one column over and kept answering directly on top of Gray. That imitation built a winning position.

slides.infoProse: This is the '5-4' central-column opening. Once Gray started column 4, Green simply kept playing where Gray played — answering on top move after move. That imitative reply blocks Gray's horizontal ideas nearby while Green's own odd-row threats keep building. Gray, to move here, is already lost.

coachMessages.text: Three separate columns, each filled by simply answering directly above the opponent's last disc. This is the Candlesticks opening — pure imitation, and a clean win.

slides.infoProse: The Candlesticks opening is the flagship example of 'I play where you play': three separated columns, each built straight up by always answering directly above the opponent's last disc. Keeping that imitative order intact hands Green a triple threat and an easy win here. But imitation is a heuristic, not a rule — Allen warns it must be checked against real threats each time; the very same column heights played in the wrong order can flip the result to the other side.

wrong1.text: Not quite — look for the right square. Try again.

correct.text: Exactly — play where they play. Answering directly above Gray's last disc keeps the imitation going.
